en: An Elucidation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* Composed by Zhenke There is no dharma outside the mind;
this is the true word of the Tathāgata. There are no waves outside water; this is the poignant metaphor of the Sage. It is only that sentient beings, from...
Since beginningless time, the habitual tendencies of names and words have been so deeply stained as to be difficult to transform. Thus, hearing of the ordinary, one clings to the ordinary;

hearing of the holy, one clings to the holy; hearing of existence, one clings to existence; hearing of non-existence, one clings to non-existence; hearing of birth-and-death, one clings to birth-and-death; hearing of nirvana, one clings to nirvana; hearing of the world, one clings to the world;
hearing of the multitude of atoms, one clings to the multitude of atoms. Consequently, the fundamental mind becomes utterly obscured.

Driven by names and words, they cling to them and forget their original source, burying their own true nature. Therefore, at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata preached the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*:
by means of the world itself he shattered the multitude of atoms, and by means of the multitude of atoms he shattered the firm habitual tendencies of the world.
Once these firm habitual tendencies are shattered, the habit of atoms is eliminated. One is lost and two are forfeited; once both one and two are lost, [the ultimate is revealed].
The original mind is suddenly revealed; thus the Sixth Patriarch said: "Do not think of good, do not think of evil—what is that which is the true face of Elder Ming?
This old master pointed directly at the person within the states of good and evil. One who understands this state beyond good and evil has many names for it:
it is called the original nature (*prakṛti*), the true mind (*bhūtamanas*), or the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

It is said that this refers to "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*) and so forth. Therefore, those with profound innate capacity (*deva-mati*) are not defiled by names and words; they are able to awaken to names and words through names and words themselves.
Those who are inferior, however, rely on this sutra to address the mentalities of the multitude of world-dusts.

Through the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he uses the multitude of world-dusts to shatter the world, showing it to have a name but no reality, and uses the world to shatter the multitude of world-dusts.
The multitude possess names but lack reality; ultimately, both name and reality are non-existent. When emotional attachments dissolve, one’s nature is restored.

Furthermore, through the Sixth Patriarch’s [teaching on] the emotions of good and evil, one awakens to the original face that is inherently free from good and evil; from the very beginning, there is no distinction.
Viewed from this perspective, if one cannot achieve immediate awakening through names and words, one will be defiled by those names and words and fail to attain the truth—not only in this world...

The elements (*dhātu*) are themselves a single composite phenomenon; even the multitude of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) is likewise a single composite phenomenon. Why is this? Because their conceptual attachments have not yet been shattered.

Therefore, I say: "To lose one is to forfeit both. Thus, you members of this assembly have gathered here on the shores of Lake Mǎo to form the karmic conditions for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
This is not a matter of uprooting sprouts from the ground; rather, it is because these individuals have, over many lifetimes, been in close proximity to various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, they encountered this by chance. A man of the Way remains detached from the world, having no initial desire for anything else. Now, at this late hour when all is quiet, amidst the light of a white candle, he does not spare his verbal karma.
Regarding both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, he lowers the high to meet the low, employing various analogies to explain them in detail.

This section of the sutra provides a detailed analysis. Although the capacities and stages of maturity among the various practitioners differ—such that some may gain entry upon hearing a practitioner’s brief comment or reminder, while others may not—the one who understands shall, from this day forward, progress from the coarse toward the subtle.

Once one has attained mastery, one will necessarily enter the divine. Once one can enter the divine, then all names and words—worlds, atoms, sages and ordinary beings, good and evil—their very handles are in one’s own hands.
How could those names and words ever turn me? Those who do not yet understand must resolve this from this day forward;
only then will you not have failed this chance encounter within the atmosphere of Yao’s legacy. Furthermore, I am old and ill.
One does not make appointments with others; the spreading fragrance cannot be grasped or toyed with. In both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, one must each exert effort.

The emotional calculations of sentient beings do not allow for "this" or "that," nor for "sage" or "ordinary person. Therefore it is said: when the emotions of sage and ordinary person are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed in its essence.
Now, though the world may be shattered and fine dust may be recombined, the world and the fine dust have never, from the beginning, existed as separate entities.
It is eternal. Yet, amidst this state where there has never been anything that begins as eternal, sentient beings reckon the world to be one and reckon atoms to be many;
they hold that what is not one must be many, and what is not many must be one. They indulge in these calculations without awakening, from time immemorial.

As for the present day—dying here and being born there, dying there and being born here—if one investigates the reason for this, it does not go beyond the failure to empty the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the consequent clinging to whatever is encountered.
Therefore, the Tathāgata said: "A unified aggregate (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) is ultimately ineffable. Yet ordinary beings greedily cling to such things.
As for those of sharp faculties, if they know that the world exists by the aggregation of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), would the world then truly exist?
Alas! If one were to shatter the world into subtle atoms, would those atoms truly exist? Alas! This lies in self-awakening;
it does not lie in the value of verbal exposition. Therefore, in this sutra, the Tathāgata raises the banner of non-arising amidst the arising of conditions;
this is the true, profound, great compassion.
Now, when one shatters the world into a multitude of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*), do these subtle particles truly exist?
When one combines a multitude of subtle particles to form a world, does this world truly exist? These two states act as subject and object to one another, mutually washing away each other;
how could the relationship between the one and the many require the beating and rinsing of celestial winds and ocean waves before it is cleansed? Therefore, one who is skillfully adept—
As for that mind, though it dwells all day long amidst the one and the many, the one and the many cannot burden it.
Those who act contrary to this cannot withstand such burdens. Therefore, this sutra says: "That which is a unified whole is not a unified whole; it is called a unified whole.
Yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things because they do not comprehend that the one and the many are impermanent. This is the essence.
This is because guests have no fixed nature. If one can penetrate this principle, then even the "single unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) has never failed to be a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Su Dongpo once said: "The sound of the mountain stream is itself the broad and long tongue [of the Buddha].
I would say: "The single unified mark is itself the broad and long tongue. Some may consider Dongpo correct and me incorrect; others may consider me correct and him incorrect.
To consider Master Chang’s position as incorrect is what is called "not speaking of dreams before a fool.
Whether one examines the world and the multitude of atoms through their mutual interplay, they are merely names and words; both lack intrinsic nature.
To say that the world exists by combining with the multitude of atoms, or that the multitude of atoms exists by the disintegration of the world—both are the deluded projections of sentient beings.

This is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Yet, this transverse construction is not without its cause; it arises because one’s engagement with phenomena is not refined and one’s penetration into principle is not thorough.

If phenomena were refined, one would be able to realize that there is no principle apart from phenomena. If principle were thoroughly penetrated, one would be able to realize that there are no phenomena apart from principle.
If there is no principle apart from phenomena, do phenomena truly exist? If there are no phenomena apart from principle, does principle truly exist? Therefore, as for nature...

The School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna) does not achieve perfection until the School of Principle (Dharmatāyāna) begins; the School of Characteristics does not achieve perfection until the School of Nature (Svabhāvayāna) begins its completion.
Because perfection is precisely refinement, one is refined yet free from conceptual thought. Because refinement is precisely perfection, one is perfect yet distinct and clear.

Because there is no conceptual thought, one accords with reality within phenomena. Because there is distinct clarity, one illuminates thoroughly within principle. Such enjoyments bring fulfillment to both self and others; however, they are easily understood while still on the path of causes.
It is difficult to realize while in the causal stage; once realized within the fruit, it is easy to realize but difficult to forget. Alas!
To enjoy it while in the causal stage, yet to forget its enjoyment within the fruit—this is something that those who wear fur and horns cannot achieve.
Now, the four views of self, person, sentient being, and life-span are originally but a single view of self.

Through successive and transverse conceptualizations, they eventually become four views. If one observes with the eye of wisdom, then the single mind does not arise; since even "self" does not exist, who is there to hold the view of self?
Once the view of self is uprooted, the remaining views will naturally become empty without waiting for them to be dispelled. Furthermore, regarding the view of self...
The "view of a self" (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) refers to forcibly positing a sovereign master where none exists. The "view of a person" (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) refers to arising in dependence upon a self;
the "view of a sentient being" (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*) refers to following emotional attachments and conceptual discriminations without being able to reflect back upon oneself.

The "view of a life-span" (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*) is nothing more than the thought of craving for birth and fearing death. Viewed in this light, the four views described in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* do not actually exist within the sūtra itself.
This occurs right within the midst of our daily activities, amidst the fluctuations of favorable and adverse circumstances; what has it to do with the Buddha?
Nevertheless, had it not been for this old fellow Gautama who skillfully pierced through with his indirect teachings, this vast expanse of the world would never have dawned from its eternal darkness.
The Buddha asked Subhūti: "If someone were to grind the trichiliocosm into a multitude of fine dust particles, would that multitude of dust particles be called many?
Subhūti replied: "It would be very many. By this, I know Subhūti’s intention:
he considers them not merely many, but upon close observation and examination, they truly exist only in name and lack substantial reality.
Therefore it is said: "That which is not a collection of atoms is called a 'collection of atoms. Furthermore, the meaning of a 'world' is likewise merely a name without reality.
Thus it is said: "That which is not a world is called a 'world. For atoms have no inherent substance of their own; they exist only when a world is broken down.
A world likewise has no inherent substance of its own; it is formed only by the aggregation of atoms. Therefore...

When one observes the world through the lens of atoms, the world appears while the atoms do not. When one observes the world through the lens of atoms, the atomic forms appear while the world does not.
If one calculates them as many fragmented aspects, then many fragmented aspects appear; if one calculates them as a single unified aspect, then a single unified aspect appears.
"Many fragmented aspects" is merely another name for atoms, and "a single unified aspect" is simply a different designation for the world.

If the capacity of the practitioner were such that they could achieve sudden and complete realization, then both the manifold aspects and the single unified aspect would all possess names but lack substantial reality;

thus, the conceptual attachments to "one" and "many" would be exhausted of themselves without waiting for them to be swept away. Once the attachments to "one" and "many" are exhausted, the mind’s inherent luminosity will manifest clearly before one.
Therefore it is said: "When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the essence reveals the true permanence. Furthermore, this...
When an object-condition arises as one, it is called "single emotion"; when it arises from many conditions, it is called "multiple emotions.

When it arises from ordinary things, it is called "ordinary emotion"; when it arises from the holy, it is called "holy emotion. Thus, whether one or many, ordinary or holy, these do not exceed the horizontal conceptualizations of a single emotion.
This is also called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*) and also called "the perception of the characteristics of external objects" (*viṣaya-nimitta-saṃjñā*).
It is further said that "the reflected shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects" are all alternative names for this very emotion.
Guifeng categorized this section of meaning as "realizing the Dharma-realm"—how profound and flavorful this is!
Where there is contraction, there is expansion; where there is accumulation, there is dispersion;
where there is union, there is fragmentation—this is the natural law. Therefore, the Tathāgata called out to Subhūti and said to him:
"If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to be broken down into atoms, would that multitude of atoms be many or few? Subhūti, receiving the Buddha’s [instruction]...

He replied, "Very many. Now, if one were to shatter the great trichiliocosm into fine motes of dust and compare them with the mental capacity of an ordinary person, they would be more numerous than that person could conceive.
Yet, from the perspective of what the Tathāgata knows, they would be fewer than he can encompass.
Is it that the Tathāgata does not know the number of these motes, such that he must wait for Subhūti to determine it? It is because the Tathāgata...
He anticipated that although all sentient beings differ in having faculties that are dull or sharp, they have never differed in their grasping at the world as a single, unified whole.

However, as soon as sentient beings with sharp faculties hear that the world can be broken down into atoms, they do not need to wait for Subhūti to say, "Many atoms are not a multitude of atoms. This is because...
They are called a multitude of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). Only then does one realize that a world is certainly not a single unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).
Alas, for sentient beings of dull faculties, it is necessary to wait for Subhūti to secretly shatter their attachment to the multiplicity of these subtle particles;
only then will they know that what was initially not a world at all is merely a world formed by the aggregation of many particles. Since the world is thus an aggregation of particles...

If it were only through aggregation that there could be a "single integrated appearance," then while the world abides as a single integrated appearance, its abiding would fundamentally be non-abiding and its integration fundamentally non-integration;
how could one wait until the world is shattered into a multitude of atoms before the single integrated appearance is finally destroyed?
Furthermore, Subhūti, I and the Tathāgata have taken this world and ground it into fine dust, and having combined those fine particles, we have reconstituted the world.

Through this process of repeated combining and crushing, repeatedly overturning and surging, those of superior faculties and those of middling faculties have already realized that the world is fundamentally non-existent;
it exists only through the combination of fine particles, yet even those fine particles are non-existent, and the world exists only through the shattering of the world. Up to this point—
Thus, the attachment to the notions of "one" and "many" does not require the contemplation of emptiness to be shattered.
Yet, because those of inferior faculties find it difficult to awaken, Subhūti again takes up the point that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is "not a world-system;
it is merely named a world-system," and informs them clearly, saying: "If the world-system were truly existent, it would be a unified mass (*ekapiṇḍa*). The world...
If the realms were a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*), then the Tathāgata has previously stated that a unified whole is precisely not a unified whole;

it is only nominally called a unified whole. Why is this so? It is because the Tathāgata and Subhūti, out of compassion for sentient beings whose attachments are difficult to shatter—who savor and cling to this body, reckoning it to be substantially real—have explained this matter in detail and at length for the sake of those of inferior faculties.
Because their grasping at existence and their misconceptions were not yet exhausted, the Tathāgata called out to Subhūti and addressed him again, saying:
"That which is a 'unified mass' (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) is ultimately ineffable; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.
Does this mean that Subhūti did not know that a unified mass is not, in fact, a unified mass, and only came to understand it after the Tathāgata had addressed him a second time? It is because...

The Tathāgata, borrowing the voice of Subhūti, deeply rebukes those of inferior faculties who cling to the body manifest before them, falsely asserting it to be substantially existent and savoring that attachment.
Alas! First, he shattered the world into subtle atoms; then, he examined those subtle atoms and found them to be non-existent.

Since atoms do not exist, the world has no substance. Therefore, Subhūti does not first refute the attachment to a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-saṃjñā*), but first refutes the attachment to multiple atoms.
For once the multiple atoms are refuted, the attachment to the unified whole is refuted without even needing to be addressed.
Why is this? Because the many constitute a single entity; when the many are refuted, the one lacks substance.
Once all deluded attachments are exhausted, both the world and its minute particles are entirely the pure Dharma-realm. What object could one point to as being the world or its minute particles?

If a student understands this, only then will they truly comprehend the bitter heart of our effort—the Tathāgata and his son—to overturn, analyze, and dissect [the teachings]. If they understand this, then the solidity of the trichiliocosm...
To shatter it into minute particles and then recombine those particles to form a world— what difference is there from the unrolling and rolling up of a single sheet of paper,
or the gathering and dispersing of floating clouds?
Commentary on the Diamond Sutra (End)
